meta.title: Knife Making In Sanjō (With Aiba Steel) | Kenji Eats Japan
meta.description:
Special thank you to the Aiba family for their hospitality and grace while hosting us in Tsubame-Sanjō and inviting us into their world of metalworking and manufacturing. It's an experience our team will never forget!

Learn more about Aiba Steel: https://www.aiba-steel.co.jp/en/

Learn more about Vonhelmick Knife Co.: https://www.vonhelmickknives.com/ Including the Vonhelmick x Kenji Shi-Toku: https://www.vonhelmickknives.com/kenji

Kenji Eats Japan is a summer-long series inspired by my travels through Japan in April of this year. Super Frienjis on my Patreon enjoy exclusive access to written recipes from this series. Free Frienjis can enjoy accompanying articles and watch videos ad-free, including this one: https://frienji.kenjilopezalt.com/posts/knife-making-in-167560578

Watch the full series: https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PLKVyj94PRGeg&si=TlmbeVSLtjM8pR1U

transcript.text: There is a new steel coming out. I can't [music] tell you too many details, but it will be the first steel that I has been approved for cutlery use from this company in in about three decades. >> [music] >> Chefs are really nerdy about knives. They like to talk about the the blade geometry. They like to talk about the sharpening angle, the material, the hardness of the metal, the cladding, the layering, the geometry of the handle. There's all kinds of little details that go into [music] knife making. All of it I I find to be very fascinating. But what that really means is that there's no [music] such thing as a best knife. It's all a matter of sort of personal taste, you know. The only other people I've ever met who are [music] as nerdy about their metal is hair stylists. And funny enough our recent trip [music] to Tsubame-Sanjo, which is a city north of Tokyo that is well known for its metalworking. Part of the reason that we ended up there was because of scissors, because of hair stylists. Let me explain how we got there. The J. Kenji Lopez Alt team, we came to Niigata, Japan specifically to the cities of Sanjo and Tsubame along with our old friends the Hansens who have been our knife making partners for a few years now to check out the metalworking that goes on there. Gordon and I have been making this knife, the sheetoku knife, which is a knife that [music] we designed together. The idea behind the knife is that it takes a standard Japanese santoku and adds a little curve to the tip [music] which gives it another quality that allows you to sort of do western style rock chopping while still maintaining [music] all of the features of a santoku knife. It's my favorite shape for a knife, and Gordon has been making it by hand. Uh you can order it. However, the issue [music] we've been running into is that we are running out of steel. Japanese steel is difficult to [music] get, and especially very high-quality Japanese steel. It's in high demand, um and the stock that we had um was starting to run low. A friend of Gordon's, um his name is Eugene Sabourin. Um he uh had actually seen um an Instagram post of mine about uh this knife-making experience with Gordon. Uh and so he ended up taking his family to go visit Gordon and his family and make a knife together. Um Eugene happens to do a lot of business in Japan, um and through Eugene we were able to meet uh the Aibas. >> I'm Doji Aiba, uh president of Aiba Shoji Company Limited. >> [music] [music] >> The Aiba family, they've been in the metal business since [music] 1861 um in Sanjo. So they've been in this region for a very long time, uh close to 200 years. You know, they started out as hardware wholesalers, and then began selling specialty steel in the 1890s. So originally they were steel merchants, really. Um however, [music] they uh invested a lot in the um the specialization in supplying and processing of uh some of Japan's most advanced [music] specialty steels. Um and so a lot of the best steels uh for various projects, whether whether it's for knife making, [music] uh or for uh scissors, or for the machines that they use to make all of that can be found um >> [music] >> in the cities of Sanjo. When we first started this deal, uh the Ibas, you know, they're a very old-school rural Japanese >> [music] >> um family company uh that does things the old-school way. So, rather than having a Zoom meeting, rather than having a phone call, um the Ibas actually flew all the way down to Oregon and visited him at his knife shop. They stayed with his family on the farm there, and then Gordon uh and his family and the Ibas, they all drove up to Seattle, um and we all sat down and had lunch. This was my very first meeting with them. I found it amazing that even with just sort of the bare inkling of an idea of a deal going on, they um found it worth their [music] while to come all the way to uh the US and visit us. And that's just the way they like to do things, you know, they [music] they like to they they like to meet in person. Uh Mr. Iba himself has said that um it's difficult to uh make a deal with someone unless you're looking them uh in the eye. >> [laughter] [music] >> So, one of the things we were most excited about was that um there is a new steel coming out. I can't tell you too many details, but it will be the first steel that that uh has been approved for cutlery use um >> [music] >> from this company in uh in about three decades. Um and it has some really interesting properties that we're really excited about as far as [music] metalworking goes. So, the reason that we know so much about the steel is that it's actually been used um for making scissors for a while. Barbers uh are very very fond of this steel. It's extremely sharp, it's extremely hard, but it's also extremely tough, which makes it excellent for [music] making scissors and for making knives. >> [snorts] [music] >> So, the reason that we use what's called san mai steel, san means three, three layer steel, is that we want to get some of [music] the best qualities of various types of steels. So, in san mai steel, typically the the core layer, [music] the center sandwich layer, the filling of the sandwich, is going to be a very very hard, high carbon steel. And the reason for that is that you want your cutting edge to be extremely hard so that I can take an edge and maintain that edge. However, if you were to make a knife on 100% out of that material, [music] it becomes very brittle. Harder steels typically are more brittle. There's some wiggle room there, but that's sort of the general rule. And so, what the outer layers of a san mai steel do are that they provide that flexibility, that strength >> [music] >> against cracking and shattering. In that way, it's very similar to the way rebar reinforces concrete, you know, where concrete [music] has strength, has compressive strength, but rebar ensures that it doesn't [music] crack. It adds elastic strength. It adds flexibility. Ten tensile strength, that's the word, tensile strength. When you get even fancier, you can have knives with many layers. So, [music] I also make a knife that has 67 layers of steel. Um, it's made in a factory, not handmade like Gordon's are, but um, 67 layers of hard and soft soft steel um, will provide [music] you sort of that strength and flexibility um, throughout the entire uh, blade. You know, so that's the basic idea is that with with knives you're always working with materials and trying to find [music] that right combination of metals um, that will give you the strength you want and the flexibility you want. And you know, one of the fun things about working with a steel company like the Ibas with all of that knowledge um, and experience is that um, when [music] they say that there's something new coming out um, well, it's exciting to us and we can and we feel like we can trust them. There's nobody who knows metal better than they do. >> [music] [music] >> Well, a lot of our visit down to Niigata was um, with [music] the hopes of seeing some of this metal in action, but what really what ended up happening was that we got a kind of crash course in what a a town with a 400-year history of [music] uh, metalworking uh, looks like as it progresses into the modern age. We ended up having some amazing access to factories, [music] but you don't even have to go to the factories to kind of know what these cities do. >> [music] >> The ground on the sidewalk everywhere is all red from the rust from the metal that's being worked. All of the manhole covers are covered [music] in depictions of uh, metal tools that have been forged. The train station in town has a small museum that features uh, a bit of the history of metal working in this town. What's really interesting is that, you know, we have this sort of romantic idea of Japanese knife makers evolving from Japanese swordsmiths. The metal workers, the expert swordsmiths, once the samurai era was over, had no work to do and so instead they turned to [music] making cutlery. While that is true in some cases, and actually in the region of Tsubame-Sanjo in Niigata, it's actually a much more practical reason that people started working with metal here. You know, Niigata, the entire region is known as one of Japan's most fertile areas and so it's where a lot of the best rice comes from, [music] a lot of the best sake comes from, as well as wonderful beef. You know, they do aged snow beef. They have access to the Sea of Japan. So, in the 17th century, you know, Niigata was an agricultural hub. However, they had issues with flooding. Farmers' entire crops would be destroyed in these floods and so the government there decided that they wanted to introduce a second industry [music] in order to help weather these floods and so metal working was introduced. And so for a while, a lot of the traditional Japanese metal working, so nails and pins and farm tools and things that were sort of really practical, were made in Sanjo. >> [music] >> And over the years, as [music] they became experts in metal working, they started introducing as well as sort of personal grooming things, as scissors. You know, the the metal working history of Sanjo is one that's very, very practical. And what's really fascinating to me is that, much [music] like the way Japanese restaurants specialize, there's not too much sort of vertical integration >> [music] >> within the factories here. Instead, what you'll find is that a lot of factories specialize in one specific thing, and even within those factories, >> [music] >> workers are highly highly specialized. So, there'll be one worker whose job is to, you know, use the pneumatic hammer to pound the steel for the knives, to forge the to to shape the knives. There'll [music] be one worker whose job is to grind it down, and then a bunch of people who are sharpening. You know, all these different tasks get completed [music] on these knife blanks, and then in the end, you end up with a handmade product that has lots and lots of institutional knowledge that goes into it. >> [music] >> You know, and all of that sort of factors into what I would say is the storied quality of Japanese [music] cutlery. By the way, thank you so much to all of the [music] frengees and members of the cookbook club for keeping up with us. You know, it's been a real big journey for us for the past year or [music] so, sort of seeing how the company can grow, and seeing how we can best [music] provide you with recipes and food content that you enjoy while also having a good time ourselves. So, thank you so much for being part [music] of the club. And if you're not part of the club, you can head over to Patreon and join there. >> [music] >> All right, back to the steel. So, my father's side of the family actually comes from a steel town in the US. So, my grandfather on my father's side, he was a steel worker at Bethlehem Steel. >> Steel dramatically flowing from the open hearth furnace for processing into many forms and products. Today is an indispensable material. >> If you're familiar with the steel industry in Pennsylvania, Bethlehem Steel was one of the major employers in Johnstown, Pennsylvania, which is where my grandfather was from. And in its heyday, the steel company employed, I think, over 100,000 people in the area. But if you drive through Johnstown today, you find a very [music] different story because, well, Johnstown, like a lot of the steel industry, a lot of the industries in the US didn't survive globalization and so an entire industry just kind of up and left. You know, so [music] coming to Sanjo and seeing a city that has been doing this now for 400 years, but has somehow managed to weather the global changes and sort of really find a niche and I find it very fascinating to see these [music] sort of two cities that I now have some ties to that, you know, ended up following very, very different paths from each other. I'm not sure what accounts for it, but you know, I think part of it is that Japanese metalwork has >> [music] >> achieved a certain level of sort of international cachet. The Iba Steel Company, I think it's less than 10% is is cutlery and in fact a lot of the what they do is sort of heavy machinery to [music] shape specialized steel into tools that then make other tools. And I think that's one of the ways that the Iba factory and a lot of the factories around here have really managed to survive is that they've been able [music] to pivot and provide specialty services as opposed to sort of the more mass manufacturing work that was more easily outsourced from the US. One of the first stops we made was at a blacksmithing dojo and I spent some time kind of honing in on our sharpening skills. We met this chef named Oedi who holds the Guinness World Record for the longest single sheet of daikon cut from [music] a single daikon at over 50 ft. It's a skill that a sushi and sashimi chefs learn, one that I had to practice a lot when I was working at a sashimi bar, but never got particularly good [music] at. Once we got to the Iba Steel Factory itself, you know, the scale of what we were seeing was just at a whole different level. This is not a factory that just makes knives, [music] you know, that it's not a factory that just makes scissors. This is a factory that processes and shapes and >> [music] >> transforms gigantic, gigantic hunks of metal. So, they process and supply the specialty steels that [music] they then in turn give to other artisans such as Gordon to turn into knives and tools and things like that. You know, because these are essentially machines that are making machines to make machines, the scale is enormous. We saw an anvil that was at least twice as tall as I was, >> [music] >> a solid metal anvil, and with a hammer that was lifted up hydraulically 30 [music] ft before dropping down. It is easily the largest hunk of metal I've ever seen. We [music] saw people, you know, pouring molten cast iron into into sand molds to create pots and pans. We saw people hammering metal into knives. You know, what's amazing is that everything [music] from the biggest machines that were used to, you know, fashion these giant blocks of steel down to >> [music] >> a single person putting the finishing touches on the knife, all of this is, you know, done in this one small town and you can walk from shop to shop [music] and sort of follow the sort of many different paths that metal takes as it goes from here out into the world. In Sanjo City, there are several metal museums that cover the history of metalworking in the town, >> [music] >> you know, including everything from how they extract it from the mountainside so the sand that they pull out that they then heat up to extract [music] the metal from to how they then take that metal and turn it into purify it and mix it and smelt it and add various elements to turn it into the various steels that they need. It's it's [music] an amazing sort of history of knife making and an amazing history of industry. [music] You know, this industry started in this town 400 years ago and it's still the heart of the town. All [music] of this has changed and yet a lot of it has stayed the same, >> [music] >> which is something you find in a lot of sort of Japanese industry and Japanese culture. >> [music] >> So, this was [music] a a business trip and when Japanese people host you, they really host you. You know, our days from morning until late afternoon were filled with these factory visits. Um and then every night we spent the night at an onsen. So, an onsen is a a Japanese hot spring, >> [music] >> a natural mountain Um and we were staying at some of the the beautiful onsens around the mountains >> [music] >> in Niigata. You can really sort of feel the integration of water and how it interacts with everything. [music] The rivers that flow through it, the rice that's grown there, the sake that's made there, everything. Like a lot of Japanese cuisine, the cuisine in Niigata is based around what's local and seasonal, you know, hyper-local, hyper-seasonal. What's growing like on the side of that mountain over there? Each one of these meals is probably 10 to 15 courses. They start off with a number of cold vegetable preparations typically. So, these will be vegetables that were harvested from the mountains. Sometimes they're little shoots, sometimes they're little buds that are coming off. We were there in the spring, so we were having all kinds of fresh little green things. Typically, the first few courses of [music] a Japanese meal will be foods that are simmered and maybe served with a little bit of an intense broth [music] or they might be lightly pickled. Sometimes they're dressed in sort of like a a nut and miso dressing. [music] But, typically you're going to have these sort of cold vegetable dishes followed by some seafood dishes. [music] It could be sashimi, it could be sushi. You might have a piece of lightly cooked fish as well or you might have a a cold piece of lightly cooked meat. [music] And then we move on to soups and broths. So, typically there will be a clear [music] soup in the middle of a meal. Although, sometimes you might get a cloudy soup. From there you can get on to even bigger dishes. One of I think one of my favorite, >> [music] >> most memorable bites was what they call snow beef. So this is very well marbled Japanese beef that has been aged in special aging rooms that get buried under the snow for a few months and they come out in the spring and they are extremely [music] tender, extremely fatty, sort of buttery, rich, smooth, melt-in-your-mouth delicious. We had a wonderful experience where some of the chefs [music] cooked tempura. You know, when when tempura is being cooked, you know, I think we might [music] we might be used to getting tempura sort of brought out from kitchen and placed on a plate in front of us, a pile of it. You know, if you go to like [music] a an American style Japanese restaurant where there is a bunch of different dishes on the menu. In Japan, typically when you get tempura, it will be fried right in front of your face and it will be handed to you so that you can eat it when it is fresh out of the fryer, which is the best way to enjoy tempura. So we ate a whole bunch of seasonal greens and little fish as well that were fried in tempura in the dining room and sort of handed us to handed to us to enjoy as soon [music] as they were done frying. Tempura I find to be one of the best ways to enjoy seasonal vegetables. You know, a tempura batter when it's done right is thin and crisp and light enough >> [music] >> that your vegetables will really shine through. That said, of course there is also sort of Japanese fast food, there's [music] Japanese comfort food. One of the specialties in Sanjo, Sanjo City is curry ramen. So >> [music] >> curry udon is a very common Japanese dish, you know, so it's essentially udon noodles, [music] thick wheat noodles that are served in a sort of thick broth. You know, so not as thick as like the curry broth that you curry sauce that you would get on katsu curry, but thicker than a typical ramen broth with that same sort of katsu curry [music] flavor. Curry ramen, kare ramen, was something I'd never seen before and is a specialty of Sanjo. Similarly, they serve a sort of thickened curry broth along with slices of pork and simmered onions uh some really chewy ramen noodles. I think it's a it's a [music] delicious dish that I think I would probably come back and make at home as well because I love curry udon and I love ramen. >> [music] >> You know, as a as a chef, you think about where your knives are coming from and you think about um the materials that go into them. Uh however, you know, I've never had access to [music] the factories like this. I've never had insight into the actual process the way um we were able to experience it here. Um and it really changes a lot about the [music] way um I think about knives. Knowing that knives that I have in my drawer here started [music] their life in this mountain over there and um went through all of these different steps and went through all of these different sort of practiced uh expert hands [music] before um arriving um in my kitchen for me to use it. When you first start eating food, if if you don't cook too much, like you don't really think about how the food arrived there. [music] And even if you do cook a lot, you often don't think about how it got from the farm uh to where you [music] are. You know, and so in the same way that I find it fascinating that chefs are able to sort of take recipes um and and foods that exist um and [music] help encourage their uh evolution and in that way, you know, a a dish can sort of survive even um as things change around it. So, you know, the the Ibas, despite being this um old old steel family [music] uh that's been in the business for generations, they are still looking to innovate >> [music] >> um and they're still looking to slowly but surely improve on materials and sort of the technology and science behind uh what goes into knife making and and you know, if we're lucky, um maybe a small piece [music] of um you know, that Ibas steel history is going to make its way uh into one of our knives in the future. Um uh guys, gals, non-binary pals, see you next time. Mhm. >> Hey.
